title: fix(cli): parse_since panics on oversized --older-than in log prune and drive lease prune
body:
## Problem

`parse_since` (`src/cli/log/query.rs:174-192`) uses the panicking `chrono::Duration::days`/`weeks` constructors and `Utc::now() - dur`, so an oversized but `i64`-valid `--older-than` crashes the process with exit 101 instead of returning the "invalid --older-than" error the commands promise. Both `omni-dev log prune` (pre-existing) and the new `omni-dev drive lease prune` (which reuses the helper at `src/cli/drive/lease.rs:278`) are affected.

## Evidence (reproduced by execution)

```
$ omni-dev drive lease prune --older-than 100000000d --dry-run
thread 'main' panicked at src/cli/log/query.rs:191:8: `DateTime - TimeDelta` overflowed

$ omni-dev drive lease prune --older-than 9999999999999999w --dry-run
thread 'main' panicked at .../chrono-0.4.45/src/lib.rs:717:17: TimeDelta::weeks out of bounds
```

`omni-dev log prune` panics identically on the same inputs. `prune_rejects_an_invalid_older_than` only covers the non-numeric case.

## Scope

`src/cli/log/query.rs`.

---
Found in a code review of the ADR-0080 Drive write-lease range `4c7185c9^..fe550423` (2026-09-10 to 2026-09-15), reviewed 2026-09-17. Line numbers are at `fe550423`.

title: gmail render: adopt the shared Selection filter from gmail insert
body:
## Context

#1655 (`gmail insert`) added `src/cli/gmail/selection.rs` — a `Selection`/`SelectionArgs` pair filtering `manifest.jsonl` by `--all`/`--since`/`--until`/`--id`/`--ids-from`/`--source-label`. It was built as a shared module specifically so `gmail render --archive-dir` could adopt it later, per its own doc comment:

> Factored out as its own module (rather than inlined into `insert.rs`) so `render` can adopt it later — a follow-up, not part of this change.

## Problem

`gmail render --archive-dir DIR --all` (`src/cli/gmail/render.rs`) currently has exactly one selector: `--all`, over every non-deleted manifest record. There's no way to render only messages in a date range, or a specific set of ids, without first filtering them into a directory of `.eml` paths some other way.

## Non-goals

- No change to `render`'s bare-file-paths mode (`omni-dev gmail render *.eml`), which has no `--archive-dir` involvement at all.

Ref #1655.

title: refactor(drive): lease ledger lock is ledger-global, non-waiting, Drop-unlinks-by-path; prune deletes backup before locking
body:
## Problem

The lease ledger lock (`LedgerLock`, `src/drive/lease/ledger.rs`) is a single `create_new` marker file per **ledger**, not per file, non-waiting, released only by `Drop` unlinking by path. Since every engine holds the `LeaseGrant` (and so the lock) across its mutating HTTP call, the consequences compound:

1. **Unrelated leased writes hard-fail.** A `drive sheets write X --lease A` in one terminal makes a concurrent `drive docs write Y --lease B` fail with "another `drive lease` operation appears to already be in progress" for the whole duration of A's upload. No wait, no retry.
2. **The error's own advice reopens the double-spend.** The message says "remove the lock file and retry". If the user does that while A is genuinely live, B acquires and creates a new marker; when A finishes, its `Drop` unlinks B's marker by path with no identity check; C can now acquire while B is mid-write, and both can pass their staleness checks against the same recorded version. The same advice and `Drop` shape exist in `src/cli/gmail/insert/ledger.rs:190-223`.
3. **A SIGKILLed or OOM-killed holder leaves a permanent lock** with no stale-lock detection (contrast `daemon/single_instance.rs`, which has a ping probe and reclaim).
4. **`drive lease prune` deletes the backup before taking the lock.** `clear_backup` runs first (`prune.rs:272`), then the per-row `mutate_locked` (`prune.rs:284`) fails rather than waits on contention, so a routine collision with an in-flight leased write leaves a row pointing at an irrecoverably deleted `Bytes` backup and aborts the rest of the batch. The error text tells the operator to act "once the underlying issue is fixed", but a lock collision has no underlying issue.
5. **`impl Drop for LedgerLock` is a bare `let _ = remove_file(...)`** (`ledger.rs:365-368`) with no log and no comment, against STYLE-0018. A failed unlink here produces the misleading "already in progress" message on the next run.
6. (Minor) `paths::create_new_file_0600` leaves the exclusively created file on disk if the follow-up `fchmod` fails (`paths.rs:182-196`), a phantom lock. Near-unreachable on local filesystems because the file is created with mode 0600 and `fchmod` only runs when group/other bits are set; the gmail lock previously had no chmod at all, so the migration was a net improvement.

## Evidence

- `ledger.rs:336-362` acquire; `ledger.rs:365-369` Drop; `ledger.rs:346-352` message text; `ledger.rs:314-318` lock path derived from the ledger path.
- Grant held across the mutation at all 8 call sites: `content_edit.rs:290/327`, `sheets/write.rs:377/427`, `sheets/format.rs:624/660`, `sheets/structure.rs:695/740`, `sheets/validation.rs:420/453`, `sheets/protection.rs:510/546`, `docs/write.rs:502/562`, `lease/restore.rs:488/582`.
- `ledger::tests::mutate_locked_refuses_while_another_lock_is_held` pins the hard-fail.
- ADR-0080 §4 chose this lock "mirroring `InsertLedger`'s `LedgerLock` exactly"; it does not state that the lock is ledger-global rather than per-file.

## Scope

`src/drive/lease/ledger.rs`, `src/drive/lease/prune.rs`, `src/cli/gmail/insert/ledger.rs`, `src/daemon/paths.rs`, ADR-0080 §4.

---
Found in a code review of the ADR-0080 Drive write-lease range `4c7185c9^..fe550423` (2026-09-10 to 2026-09-15), reviewed 2026-09-17. Line numbers are at `fe550423`.

Related: #1690 (acquire ordering), #1700 (extract the shared ledger/lock once for both ledgers)

title: gmail sync-all: per-account summary line/progress bar can be silently dropped due to MultiProgress race
body:
## Summary

`omni-dev gmail sync-all` can silently drop an account's per-account summary line (and its progress bars) from terminal output, even though that account's sync completed successfully and its counts are correctly folded into the final `combined:` total. This looks like data loss but is purely a terminal-rendering race — no actual sync/data issue.

## Repro

Run `gmail sync-all` across 5+ configured accounts (concurrency > 1) where multiple accounts finish sync around the same time. Example observed output (account names anonymized to match a 5-account config):

```
jky.greens: 2 fetched, 0 errors
777.punchbowl: 1 fetched, 2 labels updated, 0 errors
chateau.de.ky: 3 fetched, 1 labels updated, 0 errors
newhoggy: 348 fetched, 3 vanished, 4 labels updated, 0 errors
newhoggy ######## 351/351 messages fetched
chateau.de.ky ######## 3/3 messages fetched
combined: 361 fetched, 3 vanished, 29 labels updated, 0 errors
```

Only 4 of the 5 configured accounts (`jky.greens`, `777.punchbowl`, `chateau.de.ky`, `newhoggy`) got a printed summary line; the 5th (`prosperacommercial`) never printed a line or progress bar at all. However:

- Sum of the 4 printed accounts: 354 fetched, 7 labels updated
- `combined:` total: 361 fetched, 29 labels updated
- Difference (361-354=7 fetched, 29-7=22 labels updated) exactly matches a plausible contribution from the missing 5th account

So `prosperacommercial` synced successfully and its counts reached `combined`, but its own terminal output was lost.

## Root cause

Two independent tasks both redraw the same shared `indicatif::MultiProgress` for a given account, with no ordering guarantee between them:

1. The main loop prints that account's summary line via `multi.suspend(...)` when its sync task completes (`src/cli/gmail/sync_all.rs:316`).
2. A separate per-account render task (`src/cli/gmail/sync_all.rs:282`, `render_tasks.push(tokio::spawn(bars.drain(rx)))`) calls `finish_and_clear()` / `finish()` on that account's bars once its event channel closes (`src/cli/gmail/sync/progress.rs:113-114`).

Both are triggered by the same underlying event — `run_one_account` returning, which drops `progress_tx` and closes the channel (`src/cli/gmail/sync_all.rs:294-296`) — but they run as two independent Tokio tasks with no join point between them. `MultiProgress::suspend` clears all bars, runs its closure, then redraws, but has no way to coordinate with a concurrent `finish()`/`finish_and_clear()` call from the render task. Whichever redraw wins the race can clobber output the other just wrote.

The code only awaits all `render_tasks` (guaranteeing bars are settled) before printing the final `combined:` total (see the comment around `src/cli/gmail/sync_all.rs:323-328`) — there's no equivalent guarantee before each individual per-account summary print during the loop. That gap is what lets an account's own line/bars get silently dropped while its data still reaches `combined` correctly (the `outcomes` used for `combined` are populated independently of the printing).

## Suggested fix directions

- Await/join a given account's render task before (or as part of) printing its summary line, so the two redraws for that account can't race.
- Alternatively, serialize all prints and bar-finish calls through a single coordinating point (e.g. have the render task itself perform or trigger the summary-line print for its account after `finish_and_clear()`, rather than having the main loop do it independently).

## Impact

Cosmetic/observability only — no data loss. But it's misleading: a user watching the output can reasonably conclude an account was skipped entirely, when it actually synced fine.

Environment: `omni-dev 0.41.0 (b37b0aed 2026-08-25)`, macOS, `gmail-sync.yaml` `concurrency: 20`, 5 configured accounts.

title: Drive: create/upload/edit file content, gated by a new folder-scoped write-permission system
body:
## Summary

Add the ability to **create files, upload local content, and edit existing files' content** in Google Drive, gated behind a new **folder-scoped write-permission system**: disabled by default, configured per Drive account as an allow-list of folder IDs (each optionally recursive into subfolders) mapped to the specific operations permitted there. Read stays allowed everywhere by default, but the same rule schema lets it be restricted per folder too.

This is **not** a greenfield Drive feature. `omni-dev` already has a Drive integration:

- [ADR-0069](../docs/adrs/adr-0069.md) shipped Drive read-only (`drive.readonly`), with named multi-account storage mirroring Gmail's.
- [ADR-0070](../docs/adrs/adr-0070.md) added the integration's first write capability — `drive rename`/`drive move` — under an additive `drive.metadata` scope (`files.update` on `name`/`parents` only, **no file-content access**), gated by a visibility-diff safety check (moving a file can change who can see it).

Both existing write operations are metadata-only by design; there is still no way to create a new file, push local content into Drive, or change an existing file's *content*. This issue proposes that capability plus the permission system to bound it, sized and shaped to sit alongside ADR-0069/ADR-0070 rather than duplicate or reopen their decisions.

## Context

Nothing in the current surface (`src/drive/{client,auth,files_api,rename,file_move,visibility,permissions_api}.rs`, `src/cli/drive/{rename,move_file}.rs`) touches file content, and `drive.metadata` (the only write scope granted today) technically *cannot* — Google's own scope restricts `files.update` under it to the `name`/`parents` fields. Content creation/upload/edit needs a materially broader OAuth grant, which is also why this needs its own local safety gate: Google's OAuth scopes are all-or-nothing across a user's whole Drive — there is no Google-side way to say "this credential may only write inside folder X." The folder+subfolder permission model this issue proposes is `omni-dev`'s own policy layer, filling exactly that gap, the same way ADR-0070's visibility-diff gate exists because Google's `move` API itself doesn't warn you when a move changes who can see a file.

Two Google OAuth scopes are relevant, and neither alone covers everything asked for here:

- `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file` — **per-file** access, restricted by Google to files this app itself created (via this scope) or that the user explicitly picked through a Drive file picker (not applicable to a headless CLI). Sufficient for creating new files/folders and uploading new content, and for later editing *those same, app-created* files. **Not** sufficient to edit a file that already existed in the user's Drive before `omni-dev` touched it.
- `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive` (the unrestricted "full" scope) — the only scope that can edit arbitrary pre-existing file content. Substantially broader than anything this integration has requested before; it also subsumes read, unlike `drive.metadata` (see ADR-0070 §1).

So "create files, upload files, edit files" actually spans two different privilege tiers, and the design below keeps them as two independent, additive opt-ins — mirroring how ADR-0070 kept `drive.metadata` additive over `drive.readonly` rather than a replacement.

title: Support GitLab alongside GitHub (MR/pipeline parity via glab)
body:
## Summary

omni-dev's GitHub integration (PR discovery/creation, batched CI-check polling in the daemon's `worktrees` service, rate-limit-aware throttling, merge-queue enqueue, VS Code tree UI) is entirely GitHub-specific today — it shells out only to `gh`, with GitHub's GraphQL schema and REST shapes hardcoded throughout. This issue proposes adding equivalent **GitLab** support (via `glab`, GitLab's official CLI) with the same functional coverage, and lays out the redesign this requires — because several of the mechanisms that make the GitHub integration cheap **do not port as-is** and need GitLab-native replacements, not direct translations.

This was researched in depth (codebase inventory + live-verified GitLab platform research against gitlab.com and 5 self-managed instances) before writing this plan. Findings below are sourced; anything not independently verified is marked `[U]`.

---

## Part 1 — What exists today (GitHub-only)

omni-dev never talks to the GitHub REST/GraphQL API directly (no `octocrab`, no direct `reqwest` to `api.github.com` — confirmed via `Cargo.toml`/grep). Every integration point shells out to `gh`, chosen specifically so the GitHub token never enters the omni-dev process (ADR-0003, ADR-0050).

| Mechanism | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `gh` binary resolution | `src/pr_status.rs` (`resolve_gh_binary`, `OMNI_DEV_GH_BIN`) + TS twin `editors/vscode/src/gh.ts` | env → well-known paths → `PATH` |
| Remote → "is this GitHub?" detection | `src/git/remote.rs` (`extract_github_repo_name`) **and independently** `src/daemon/services/worktrees.rs` (`GithubIdentity`/`github_identity`) | Two separate hardcoded `"github.com"` string-matching implementations — should be unified regardless of GitLab work |
| PR discovery | `gh pr list` (`src/cli/git/info.rs`, `src/daemon/services/worktrees.rs`'s `OpenPrCache`, TTL 60s) | |
| PR creation/update | `gh pr create` / `gh pr edit` (`src/cli/git/create_pr.rs`) | |
| **Batched PR+check status poll** | `src/pr_status.rs` — one `gh api graphql` call per cycle, **aliasing** `repository(owner,name){ pullRequest(...) }` for up to ~50-100 (repo,branch) pairs at ~1 GraphQL point total | The core cost-saving trick; GitHub-specific (see Part 3) |
| Rate-limit monitor | `src/github_rate_limit.rs` — polls `gh api rate_limit` every 60s (a call GitHub documents as free/uncounted); throttles poll cadence when any resource ≥80% used | |
| Merge queue | `src/daemon/services/worktrees.rs` `merge-queue` op (ADR-0056) — wraps GitHub's native repository merge-queue product feature | |
| Request-log accounting | `src/github_metrics.rs` (`run_gh`, the one choke point), `RecordKind::Gh` | `omni-dev log count --kind gh`, `daemon service github summary` |
| VS Code tree UI | `editors/vscode/src/{github,gh,prCommands,prClipboard,repoCommands,tree}.ts` — PR badges, "Open GitHub Repository", "Copy PR URL", "Open Pull Request" (hands off to the `GitHub.vscode-pull-request-github` marketplace extension by URI scheme) | Hard external dependency on that specific extension for in-editor MR/PR viewing |

**Already provider-agnostic** (reusable as-is): the four-state `PrCheckState` (`success|failure|pending|none`) and everything downstream of it (badge rendering, `rowColorId`, decorations); the daemon's generic subscribe/diff/change-notify plumbing; `TreeSnapshotCache`/`OpenPrCache`/`RateLimitCache`'s lease/TTL *patterns* (not their GitHub-specific payloads); the `test_support::shim` fake-binary test harness used for `gh` (directly reusable for `glab`).

**Explicit prior scope statement to revise:** `docs/worktrees-service.md` currently states outright: *"PR badges are `gh`-based and GitHub-only (#1296)… Other forges (GitLab/Bitbucket)… are out of scope."* This issue proposes changing that.

---

title: feat(daemon): native (non-WSL) Windows port of the daemon control plane and clients
body:
## Summary

Track the work to run the omni-dev **daemon** — and the CLIs and VS Code companion
that talk to it — natively on **Windows, outside WSL**.

Split out from #1237, which fixed the *documentation* problem (the closed #1041 was
miscited as the Windows tracker; corrected in #1241) and concluded that **WSL2 is the
supported way to run the daemon on Windows and needs no code**. This issue is the
tracker for the remaining, larger effort: a **native** Windows toolchain.

## Scope boundary — why WSL is already enough for most, but not this

WSL2 runs a real Linux kernel, so to omni-dev it *is* Linux: `#[cfg(unix)]` holds, the
`AF_UNIX` control socket works, the systemd user unit works, and the companion works
when VS Code is driven through **Remote-WSL** (the extension host runs *inside* WSL).
That configuration is already supported with zero changes and is **out of scope** here.

This issue covers the case WSL can't serve: a **native Windows** extension host,
terminals, and Claude Code talking to the daemon. A WSL daemon cannot serve those —
the `AF_UNIX` socket does not cross the WSL2 VM boundary (only `localhost` TCP is
forwarded between Windows and the VM), the companion's socket client
(`editors/vscode/src/socket.ts`) is Unix-domain-only with no `win32` branch, and even
with a TCP transport the Windows-vs-Linux path models would not line up.

## Work items (sketch, not yet designed)

- **Control-plane transport.** Replace `AF_UNIX` (`UnixListener`/`UnixStream` in
  `src/daemon/server.rs`, `single_instance.rs`) with a Windows-appropriate transport —
  a named pipe (`\\.\pipe\...`) or a `127.0.0.1` TCP loopback socket guarded by the
  existing bearer-token model — behind a cross-platform abstraction. Un-gate the
  currently `#[cfg(unix)]` daemon modules (`client`, `lifecycle`, `protocol`,
  `registry`, `server`, `service`, `services`, `single_instance` in `src/daemon.rs`).
- **Client transport.** `editors/vscode/src/socket.ts` needs the matching transport and
  a `win32` branch in `defaultDataDir` (today it handles only macOS + "other unix").
  The `snowflake` / `worktrees` / `sessions` CLI clients (`#[cfg(unix)]` in
  `src/cli.rs`) inherit the same Unix-only assumption.
- **Single-instance / activation.** There is no launchd (macOS) or systemd (Linux)
  analog. Decide between a Windows Service, Task Scheduler, or a plain
  detached-spawn-only model (the current off-service-manager fallback).
- **Path reconciliation (the crux beyond transport).** The worktrees/sessions services
  aggregate *paths*. A native Windows VS Code reports `C:\...` or `\\wsl$\...` UNC
  paths; `git2` enrichment must agree with what the clients report. Define canonical
  path handling so cross-window aggregation lines up.
- **CI.** A Windows compile job already exists (daemon `#[cfg(unix)]`'d out, guarding
  `cargo install` for the non-daemon commands — from #1041). Extend it to build and
  exercise the daemon on Windows.

## Already handled / non-goals

- `src/daemon/paths.rs` is already cross-platform (`dirs::data_dir()`) and stays as-is.
- WSL2 (including VS Code Remote-WSL) already works — not in scope.
- The non-daemon CLI already builds and installs on Windows — not in scope.

## Housekeeping

The four "future work (#1237)" citations (`src/daemon.rs`, `src/cli.rs`,
`docs/worktrees-service.md`, `docs/adrs/adr-0040.md`) should be repointed to this issue
so they no longer dangle at a closed one — the same dangling-reference class #1237 was
filed to fix.

title: gmail: MESSAGES_GET_COST_UNITS/GMAIL_QUOTA_UNITS_PER_SECOND are stale against current Gmail API docs
body:
## Context

While researching #1655 (`gmail insert`), the quota-unit costs and per-user rate ceiling `src/gmail/messages_api.rs` assumes were checked against Google's current Gmail API reference and found to have drifted:

```rust
pub const GMAIL_QUOTA_UNITS_PER_SECOND: u32 = 250;
pub const MESSAGES_GET_COST_UNITS: u32 = 5;
```

Google's documentation now states:
- `messages.get` costs **20** quota units, not 5.
- The per-user rate limit is **100** units/second, not 250.

These constants drive `gmail sync`'s proactive `TokenBucket` pacing (`src/cli/gmail/sync/engine.rs`) and the `MAX_CONCURRENCY`/`search_summaries` concurrency bound (`src/gmail/messages_api.rs`). If Google's current numbers are accurate, `sync`'s limiter is currently *under*-pacing relative to the real per-user ceiling — admitting up to 2.5x the actual allowed throughput — which would surface as elevated 429/`rateLimitExceeded` responses under sustained load rather than a silent failure (the client already retries those), but is worth tightening so the proactive limiter does its job instead of leaning on reactive retry.

## Non-goals

Not a behavior change beyond constant values — no new pacing mechanism, no API surface change.

Noted but deliberately out of scope for #1655 rather than folded in, since it's pre-existing and orthogonal to `gmail insert` itself.

title: test(claude): timeout_reaps_full_process_group fails on loaded macOS — 500ms budget is shorter than a cold shim exec
body:
## Problem

`claude_cli::tests::timeout_reaps_full_process_group` fails reliably on macOS when
the machine is busy, and — contrary to what it looks like — **re-running it in
isolation does not help**. It can fail 3/3 in isolation while CI is green.

## Measured mechanism

The test writes a fresh shim into a fresh `TempDir` on every run, so every run pays
a **cold `exec`**: first execution of a newly written file, page-in plus macOS's
quarantine/Gatekeeper check. Timed on a loaded machine (load average ~8.8),
executing a freshly written shim of exactly the test's shape:

```
run 1: 614 ms   <- cold
run 2:  19 ms
run 3:  19 ms
run 4:  19 ms
run 5:  19 ms
```

The client is configured with `Duration::from_millis(500)`, so the timeout fires
before `/bin/sh` reaches its `printf`, the pid file is never written, and the test
panics at:

```
shim should have recorded sleeper PID before sleeping: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound }
```

Note the assertion that actually fails is the *pid-file read*, not the timeout
assertion — the timeout error arrives as expected, which is why this reads as a
mysterious flake rather than a budget problem.

## Why it is invisible in CI

CI runs on unloaded Linux runners with no Gatekeeper, where the cold exec is far
under 500 ms. So the test is green on every PR and only bites local development —
on macOS, on a machine running parallel builds.

## Notes

Related to the shim `ETXTBSY` race that `retry_on_etxtbsy` already absorbs
(#1348) — same "freshly written shim" root cause, different symptom.

Found while releasing v0.43.0; `src/claude/ai/claude_cli.rs` and
`src/test_support.rs` are unchanged since v0.42.0, so this is long-standing rather
than a recent regression.

title: feat(jev): validate the 255-option and 10-level caps locally
body:
## Problem

`omni-dev ai jev` checks only the minimum sizes locally: at least two `choice` options and at least two `score` levels (in `choice`, `score` and in every `ask` spec). TypeSafe's docs for `jev-1.13.0` also set upper limits:

- `choice`: up to 255 options ([Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice))
- `score`: 2 to 10 levels ([Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score))

An oversized question is sent anyway, and only the API rejects it. The API error body is undocumented, so it may not say which question was too big.

## Context

Found while writing the Best practices section for #1770 (PR #1773). That PR documents the caps and says omni-dev doesn't enforce them.

title: [Feature]: Add Terminal in Editor to the terminal + menu
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

The terminal toolbar's existing **+ ▾** menu provides a convenient place to launch terminals, but omni-dev does not currently offer an entry there that opens a terminal directly in the editor area.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add a **Terminal in Editor** profile to the existing **+ ▾** menu through the omni-dev VS Code extension. Selecting it should create and focus a new shell terminal as an editor tab.

Acceptance criteria:
- The entry appears alongside the other terminal profiles in the existing **+ ▾** menu.
- Selecting it opens and focuses a new terminal in the editor area, even when launched from the terminal panel's menu.
- Each selection creates a new terminal.
- Use the user's normal shell and workspace working-directory behavior.
- Existing profiles and the default **+** action retain their current behavior.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Use the Command Palette to create a terminal in the editor area, or move an existing terminal into the editor area. A separate toolbar button was also considered; the requested entry belongs in the existing **+ ▾** menu.

### Use Case

Launch a shell directly beside source files as an editor tab using the familiar terminal creation menu.

title: sessions: the wrapper keep-alive pins finished and never-prompted chats, inflating a worktree's session count
body:
## Problem

A worktree row in the Worktrees tree shows a session cue for **more Claude
sessions than the window has chat tabs** — e.g. `⚙◦` (one working, one idle)
for a window with a single visible Claude tab.

The daemon is not miscounting: each entry corresponds to a genuinely live
`claude` process. The bad premise is Feed 4's, in
[`StreamTracker::keepalive`](src/sessions/stream.rs):

> The wrapper lives exactly as long as the `claude` process does, so this is
> real liveness rather than the activity-based approximation the hook and
> transcript feeds are limited to.

That holds for the *process* but not for the *tab*. The Claude VS Code
extension keeps a live `claude` process per chat in a window — not per visible
tab — so the 30s `KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL` in
[`claude_wrap.rs`](src/cli/claude_wrap.rs) refreshes `last_seen` for chats the
user finished hours ago, and the generous 5-minute `DEFAULT_SESSION_TTL`
([`src/sessions.rs`](src/sessions.rs)) that used to age them out never fires.

Before #1406 these sessions aged out on the TTL exactly as ADR-0052 documents.
The wrapper's process-lifetime liveness is what pins them.

There are **two** distinct phantom populations, so a single "does it have a
transcript?" rule only fixes half of it:

1. **Never-prompted spares** — a `claude` process the extension starts and
   never sends a prompt to. No transcript file is ever created.
2. **Finished chats** — a previous conversation in the same window, with a
   real transcript, whose process the extension keeps alive.

## Evidence

Observed against a live daemon (42 `omni-dev claude-wrap` processes resident
across all windows at the time).

**Population 1** — worktree `succinctly/issue-355-…`, one visible Claude tab,
two sessions reported:

| session      | state   | model            | transcript                     |
| ------------ | ------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `02661a96…`  | idle    | –                | path reported, **no such file** |
| `e5cd9b83…`  | working | claude-sonnet-5  | 440 KB, live                   |

Both map to real processes under the *same* extension host (pid 93391, window
started 23:06:54):

- wrapper pid 93503, started 23:06:55 — never prompted, no transcript
- wrapper pid 95247, started 23:07:13 — the actual conversation

Their argv is byte-identical (`diff` of both command lines is empty) and
neither carries `--resume`, so the extra process is not a resumed session.

It is **not an orphan the wrapper failed to reap**: `lsof` shows the extension
host still holding both ends of the extra wrapper's stdin/stdout socketpairs,
i.e. the extension is deliberately keeping the process alive. Signal
forwarding and stdin-EOF teardown in `claude_wrap.rs` are not implicated.

**Population 2** — worktree `succinctly/issue-462-…`, extension host pid 78511
holds **three** live `claude` processes, of which the registry surfaces two,
*both* with real transcripts:

| session      | state   | model             | transcript |
| ------------ | ------- | ----------------- | ---------- |
| `36f1441f…`  | idle    | claude-opus-5[1m] | 946 KB     |
| `c4fbfa31…`  | working | claude-sonnet-5   | 63 KB      |

The idle 946 KB one is a finished conversation, still pinned by its wrapper's
keep-alive. (The third process never emitted a `system`/`init` line carrying a
`session_id`, so `StreamTracker::request` reports nothing for it at all.)

## Impact

- The per-worktree session cue (glyphs + badge) in the Worktrees tree
  overstates how many Claude sessions a worktree is running — the user-visible
  symptom that surfaced this.
- `omni-dev sessions list` and the daemon tray's "Claude Sessions" submenu are
  inflated the same way.
- Grows over time within a long-lived window: every new chat leaves its
  predecessor's process pinned, so the count only ever goes up until the
  window is closed.
- No correctness impact on the state of the session that *is* current.

## Out of scope

- Whether the Claude VS Code extension *should* keep a process per finished
  chat — upstream behaviour, and omni-dev has to cope either way.
- Any attempt to learn which session a window's active tab is showing. The
  Claude extension exposes no API for it; ADR-0052 already records this.

## Additional context

Surfaced from a user report that a worktree with a single Claude tab was
showing a two-session cue. Related but distinct: #1451 (window tie-break),
#1447 (sessions logging).

title: drive lease prune --max-size can evict a superseded live backup ahead of its useless replacement
body:
## Problem

`prune --max-size`'s `bytes_survivors` sort (`src/drive/lease/prune.rs:243-247`) can evict a superseded token T's *real* backup ahead of the fresh lease N's *useless* pre-restore-content copy, purely because N's `expires_at` sorts later than T's.

Mechanics, worked out while adding coverage for #1742's live-T `FreshLeaseButWriteFailed` gap:

1. When a live backup token T is superseded during a restore (issue #1685's supersede — `acquire.rs`'s `insert_record`, `restore.rs:497-503`), T is released in the same locked rewrite that mints the fresh lease N. `ledger.release` (`ledger.rs:304-320`) only stamps `released_at`; it never moves `expires_at`. So T's row keeps its original, earlier `expires_at`, while N is minted with a fresh, later one.
2. If the restore's write then fails (`FreshLeaseButWriteFailed`) and N is never presented to `--lease` — it simply times out — both T and N end up non-live (`prune.rs`'s `non_live` partition, lines ~207-218: T because it's released, N because its own later `expires_at` has since passed) and become size-filter candidates together.
3. `bytes_survivors.sort_by_key(|rec| std::cmp::Reverse(rec.expires_at))` (`prune.rs:243`) sorts purely by `expires_at` descending. Since N's `expires_at` is always later than T's (it was minted after T, with a fresh full-length expiry), N sorts strictly ahead of T.
4. `keep_count_by_size` (`prune.rs:170-191`) greedily keeps the longest newest-`expires_at`-first prefix that fits the byte budget. Under a tight `--max-size`, this can keep N (the pre-restore, operationally useless copy) and evict T (the real, wanted backup) — the opposite of what an operator pruning by size would want.

`--older-than` is immune: it filters directly on `expires_at >= cutoff` per row (`prune.rs:226-230`), so it doesn't compound the two rows' *relative* order the way the bytes-budget's competitive keep does.

## Scope

`src/drive/lease/prune.rs` (`bytes_survivors` sort / `keep_count_by_size` / the `non_live` partition).

---
Split out from #1742 (per user decision during that issue's implementation: stay test-focused there, track this behavior change separately). Not currently reproduced by an automated test — the mechanics above were worked out by code reading, not exercised end-to-end.

title: fix(request-log): best-effort request-log records still land in audit.jsonl when OMNI_DEV_LOG_FILE aliases it
body:
## Problem

#1717 guards the audit log against `OMNI_DEV_LOG_FILE` aliasing it in `prune` (`request_log.rs:~1114`), `append_with_rotation` (`:~1036`) and `record_audit_to`'s own collision check (`:~751`), using `same-file` identity. But the ordinary best-effort append path is unguarded: `try_record` (`:670`) → `append_record_to(&path, …)` where `path = log_file_path()`. So with `OMNI_DEV_LOG_FILE` naming `audit.jsonl`, every `invocation`/`http` record is appended into the fail-closed forensic log. Even with rotation configured, `append_with_rotation`'s guard only withholds the rotation and still appends the line.

`record_audit`'s own doc acknowledges this: "This only stops the write into the request log; it does not stop the reverse (`OMNI_DEV_LOG_FILE` naming the audit file lets best-effort records land there too)". So it is a documented residual, not a silent oversight; it is filed because a single refusal at resolution would close it and every future consumer at once. (`cli/log/count.rs:97` and `daemon/services/github_counters.rs:120` read `log_file_path()` unguarded; those are reads and do not matter.)

## Scope

`src/request_log.rs`, `docs/log.md`.

---
Found in a code review of the lease fix wave `fe550423..8a7b8400` (PRs #1703-#1726, merged 2026-09-17/18), reviewed 2026-09-18. Line numbers are at `8a7b8400`.

Related: #1694 (the PR whose doc explicitly left this direction open)

title: fix(cli): worktrees ui can hang forever on quit when a PTY child ignores SIGHUP
Coding trainer: watch VS Code activity via the daemon and coach through an exercise (5th daemon service + MCP trainer tools)
body:
## Summary

Build a **coding trainer**: a Claude session that *watches a developer work in VS Code in
real time* and coaches them through a coding exercise. The omni-dev VS Code companion reports
editor activity to the daemon; the daemon distils it into a semantic, diff-able timeline; a new
set of `omni-dev-mcp` tools lets a Claude session **poll** that timeline and offer Socratic hints
when — and only when — something notable has changed.

omni-dev supplies the **sensing + memory**. The pedagogy (when to interrupt, how Socratic to be)
lives *outside* Rust, as a prompted Claude polling loop (a `/loop`-style skill).

This is the daemon's **fifth service** (`activity`), after browser-bridge, snowflake, worktrees,
and sessions. It deliberately reuses those services' proven shapes rather than inventing new ones.

## Motivation

A trainer needs to see what the learner is actually doing — which file they're in, what errors
they're fighting, whether tests are going green, what they just wrote — and no single vantage
point sees it: a VS Code extension host is sandboxed per window, and the transcript/git state
alone carries no live editor signal. A single resident daemon is the rendezvous point, exactly as
it already is for worktrees and sessions.

title: Add security-aware rename/move support to Drive integration
body:
## Context

`omni-dev`'s Drive integration (`src/drive/`, `src/cli/drive/`, `src/mcp/drive_tools.rs`) is
deliberately read-only today, per [ADR-0069](../../../wrk/rust-works/omni-dev/docs/adrs/adr-0069.md):
"no upload/create/rename/move/trash/share/permission-mutation capability anywhere in the surface."
The user wants to add rename and move, with move treated as security-sensitive: moving a file
between folders can change *who can see it*, because Drive resolves a file's effective access from
direct permissions on the file plus permissions inherited from its parent folder chain — and moving
a file changes that chain. Renaming only touches the `name` field and never changes `parents`, so it
never affects visibility.

Requirements (verbatim from the user): every move/rename must be logged; when there's a visibility
change, the log must capture the details; moves that would change visibility are rejected **by
default**; two independent opt-ins let a user allow a visibility *increase* and/or a visibility
*decrease*; bulk operations must work, and skip only the unsafe items when no opt-in is given rather
than failing the whole batch.

title: feat(glossary): sync team acronym definitions into a macOS Dictionary bundle
body:
## Summary

Add a `glossary` subsystem that syncs acronym definitions from GitHub and
Confluence into a normalised term index, and renders that index into a macOS
`.dictionary` bundle plus a JSON export.

The user-facing result: hover any acronym anywhere on macOS — Slack, a PR
diff, a Confluence page, a terminal — press <kbd>⌃</kbd><kbd>⌘</kbd><kbd>D</kbd>,
and get your team's definition of it.

## Motivation

Every team accumulates a private vocabulary, and the definitions almost always
already exist — scattered across a handbook repo, a Confluence space, and the
preamble of old RFCs. The problem isn't that they're unwritten, it's that
they're not available at the moment of confusion. Today the options are all
bad: interrupt someone in `#general`, dig through Confluence search, or guess.

Existing solutions don't fit:

- **Slack apps** can't do hover. Slack's platform exposes slash commands,
  shortcuts, Block Kit and unfurls — none of which give an app any hook into
  hovering over arbitrary text in a rendered message, and there is no DOM
  access. The ecosystem has converged on bots that reply in-thread.
- **Browser extensions** work but only cover `app.slack.com`, break whenever
  Slack's hashed class names churn, and do nothing for the desktop app or any
  other tool.
- **An Accessibility-API daemon** works everywhere but requires forcing
  Chromium's accessibility tree on inside Electron apps
  (`AXManualAccessibility`), which Electron's own docs warn significantly
  affects performance. Steep cost for a small ergonomic gain.

macOS already ships the delivery mechanism. Look Up is system-wide, needs no
permissions and no background process, and **has been verified to fire inside
Slack's Electron client**. Custom dictionaries drop into
`~/Library/Dictionaries` and participate fully.

So the missing piece isn't the tooltip — it's keeping the dictionary in sync
with the documents that define the terms. That's squarely omni-dev's existing
territory: it already has an Atlassian client with schema-validated ADF↔Markdown
roundtrips, a layered config chain, and CI-friendly check commands.

title: Add Claude session-state cues to the Worktrees tree via a stream-tee wrapper feed
body:
## Context

The Worktrees tree view (companion VS Code extension) shows which worktrees are open in a
VS Code window, but not what the Claude Code sessions in those windows are *doing*. The user
wants per-worktree visual cues — **how many busy / idle / waiting Claude sessions** are running
in each open worktree.
